title: You speak more Viking than you think

entries.note: Vikings who raided the English coast and then took land inland; the Anglo-Saxons used Danes for anyone speaking a Scandinavian tongue, which oversimplified things.
The large part of England where Old Norse and Old English speakers lived side by side, married and fought, so their vocabularies mixed.
From Old Norse [[from:víkingr]], pirate or sea rover, probably from [[from?:vík]]; little used in English until revived in the early 1800s; a job description, not an ethnic identity.
Old Norse word for a creek or bay, possibly the source of [[gave?:Viking]], and found in [[gave:Reykjavik]] and probably [[gave:Wick]].
Early-1800s scholars linked it to the ending of [[unrelated:Viking]] ("kings of the bay"), a theory that has since been discredited.
Old English word recorded centuries before Old Norse víkingr, thought to come from [[from?:wic]], village or camp, perhaps because raiders camped over winter.
Old English word for village or camp found in many place names; whether it is related to Old Norse [[same-root?:vík]] is debated.
Its ending is Old Norse [[from:vík]], bay, so the name means smoky bay.
Place in the north of Scotland, probably named from the Old Norse word for a bay, [[from?:vík]], since the Anglo-Saxons were not in Scotland.
Another name for the Vikings, and the meaning behind the word [[gave:Norman]].
The Normans came soon after the Vikings and were Vikings themselves; the word means [[from:Norsemen]] or Northmen, and they gave their name to [[gave:Normandy]].
Pronoun from Old Norse, replacing Old English [[see:hie]].
Pronoun from Old Norse, replacing Old English [[see:him]].
Pronoun from Old Norse, replacing Old English [[see:heora]].
Old English pronoun used where we now say [[see:they]].
Old English plural pronoun used where we now say [[see:them]]; imagine using him as the non-binary pronoun today.
Old English pronoun used where we now say [[see:their]].
A key verb from the Vikings, replacing Old English [[see:niman]].
Old English verb replaced by [[see:take]].
From the Scandinavian languages, replacing Old English [[see:bist]] and [[see:beoth]].
Old English verb form used with you, replaced by [[see:are]].
Old English verb form used with they, replaced by [[see:are]].
From Old Norse [[from:sœma]], to honour or conform to; it first meant to be fitting, then to appear to be. Compare [[same-root:seemly]].
Means decorous or fitting and keeps the older sense of [[same-root:seem]]; now a lost positive, since people mostly say [[see:unseemly]].
Still in common use, unlike its lost positive [[see:seemly]].
Verb (also to bath) from Old English, cognate with the Old Norse borrowing [[same-root:bask]].
Borrowed from Old Norse and a [[see:cognate]] of [[same-root:bathe]], with a slightly different sense.
A word with ultimately the same origin, such as [[see:bask]] and [[see:bathe]]; discussed in an earlier episode.
Raised in the unpaired words episode; a ruthless person feels no regret, from [[from:ruth]], an Old Norse word for sorrow.
Older word, found in Old English, sharing a root with [[same-root:ruth]]; to rue the day is to feel sorrow about it.
Noun from Old Norse meaning sorrow, appearing in the 1200s; paired with [[same-root:rue]] on the model of [[see:true]] and [[see:truth]]; unrelated to the name [[unrelated:Ruth (name)]].
Its pairing with [[see:truth]] was the model for pairing [[see:rue]] with [[see:ruth]].
The noun paired with [[see:true]], the model for [[see:ruth]].
The name is unrelated to [[unrelated:ruth]].
A language like the Scandinavian ones where the verb always comes second, though not necessarily in subordinate clauses.
Famous Norse warlord who landed in northern France and bullied [[see:Charles the Simple]] into giving the Vikings land that became [[see:Normandy]].
The local ruler, with an amusing name, whom [[see:Rollo]] bullied into handing over part of northern France.
The part of northern France given to [[see:Rollo]]'s Vikings, named after the [[from:Norman]]s.
A descendant of the Vikings, so the [[see:Battle of Hastings]] was more of a Germanic face-off than people think.
Anglo-Saxon king of England in 1066 who defeated [[see:Harald Hardrada]] in the north before heading south to fight [[see:William the Conqueror]].
Scandinavian king, to all intents and purposes a Viking, defeated by [[see:Harold Godwinson]] in 1066.
Harold Godwinson's fight against a 'French' army that was really quite Viking, making it more of a Germanic face-off.
As in to and fro, meaning away or backward; from Old Norse [[from:frá]], first found in Northern English and Scots, a doublet of [[same-root:from]].
The Old English doublet of the Old Norse-derived [[same-root:fro]].
Remnant of an Old Norse-style infinitive, a contraction of at and do, meaning a commotion, like a big [[see:to-do]]; compare Norwegian [[see:å (Norwegian)]].
The English infinitive particle and Old English preposition; with more Norse influence it might have been [[see:at]], and [[see:till]] took over some uses.
The particle that forms Norwegian infinitives, cognate with English [[same-root:at]], illustrating the origin of [[see:ado]].
Cognate with the Norwegian infinitive particle [[same-root:å (Norwegian)]]; with more Old Norse influence we might say at speak instead of to speak.
A big to-do means a big commotion, just as [[see:ado]] does.
Going a-hunting is ultimately at hunting, like [[see:ado]].
Preposition from Old Norse that sits beside Old English [[see:to]] with different uses; it is the original word, not a shortening of [[gave:until]].
Comes from [[from:till]], with Old Norse [[from:und]], as far as or up to, even though till is often treated as its shortening.
An Old Norse word with the sk sound Old English lacked; it replaced [[see:heaven]] as the general word for the sky.
From Old Norse; the Old English word was the unrelated [[see:hide]].
From Old Norse; the Old English equivalent was [[see:craft]].
The Old Norse equivalent of Old English [[same-root:shirt]], both meaning a short garment, and related to [[same-root:short]].
The Old English form of the word that came from Old Norse as [[same-root:skirt]]; related to [[same-root:short]].
Shares its etymology with [[same-root:shirt]] and [[same-root:skirt]], both of which originally meant a short garment.
The Old English word for what we got from Old Norse as [[see:skin]].
The Old English equivalent of the Old Norse [[see:skill]], still in use.
From Old Norse, the doublet of Old English [[same-root:ditch]]; both mean a hole in the ground.
The Old English doublet of the Old Norse [[same-root:dyke]].
From Old French [[from:escarre]], scab, from Greek [[from:eschara]], probably altered by Old Norse [[see:skarð]], a cut; also once a word for a bare rocky face.
Related to Old Norse [[same-root:skarð]], a cut; to score is to scratch, which is why score is used for counting tally marks.
England's highest hill or mountain, whose name the hosts confirm comes from Old Norse; Rob guesses its elements [[see:scar]] and [[see:fell]] give craggy hill.
A hill; it has a Scandinavian ring and is an element of [[see:Scafell Pike]].
One of several topographical words from Old Norse.
Every sense comes from an Old Norse word for an opening or void, including mythical voids like [[see:Ginnungagap]].
In Norse mythology, the yawning primordial void lying between icy [[see:Niflheim]] and fiery [[see:Muspelheim]].
The icy northern realm on one side of [[see:Ginnungagap]].
The fiery southern realm on the other side of [[see:Ginnungagap]].
Back-formed by [[see:Walter Scott]] from Old Norse [[from:berserkr]]; he thought it meant bare, but it probably means bear shirt, a warrior dressed in bearskin.
A fittingly violent word from Old Norse.
From Old Norse elements meaning house and to seek; originally searching a house legally for stolen goods, later pillaging.
The weapon, a word from Old Norse.
Thought to have been influenced by Old Norse.
One of the very unbrutal words from Old Norse.
From Old Norse, essentially bound to the house: the head of the household, usually a man; older English used [[see:wer]].
Older English word for a man or husband, surviving in [[gave:werewolf]]; paired with [[see:wif]].
Preserves the old word [[from:wer]], man.
Old English word for woman, paired with [[see:wer]] for man.
From an Old English word for a wife or woman of the household; not Old Norse.
From Old Norse [[from:angra]], to vex or distress; first a verb, a noun a century later meaning ill will or physical pain; related to [[same-root:hangnail]] and [[same-root:angst]].
Old Norse word meaning sadness or low spirits, related to [[same-root:anger]].
An injury that looks angry may preserve the old physical-pain sense of [[same-root:anger]] rather than being figurative.
Discussed before; nothing to do with hanging, its first element meant painful, sharing a root meaning tight or constricted with [[same-root:anger]].
Borrowed from the German word for fear and related to [[same-root:anger]].
Verb from Old Norse; before it, English used the word that became [[see:starve]], like German [[same-root:sterben]].
The German for to die, matching the Old English word that became [[same-root:starve]].
Once the general Old English word for to die, like German [[same-root:sterben]]; narrowed to dying from lack of food after [[see:die]] arrived.
A euphemistic Old English word for dying; compare [[see:forthgan]].
Thought to mean brown thing; the original name is unknown, possibly avoided through superstition, as Old English may have avoided a word like [[see:die]].
Sometimes used in Old English for dying, probably of a fever; it meant to burn slowly.
Old English word for dying: you have gone forth, so you are dead; compare [[see:forthfaran]].
German verb for going by some means of transport, as opposed to [[see:gehen]], on foot; English [[same-root:fare]] has the same element.
The German equivalent of go, used for going on foot, contrasted with [[see:fahren]].
As in how do you fare, an English survival of the element in German [[same-root:fahren]]; also in [[see:farewell]].
Contains [[see:fare]], one answer to a question raised a few episodes ago.
Old English expression for dying that sounds blunt now but was evidently less so then; often found in association with still water or air.
From Old Norse, originally meaning morally evil; British speakers favour it where Americans say [[see:sick]].
More common in the US than [[see:ill]]; despite its sk-like sound it is not the Old Norse word.
When a word like [[see:ill]] or [[see:sick]] becomes slang for something very good, as with [[see:bad]].
Another example of an [[see:inversion]], as in 'this podcast is really bad'.
From Old Norse [[from:uggligr]], dreadful; unusually based on fear rather than misshapenness, so it implies looks that strike dread.
English suffix from Old English -lic, like, cognate with the second element of the Old Norse source of [[see:ugly]].
From Old Norse [[from:vrangr]], crooked, from a root meaning curved; it moved from bent to unjust, a fitting opposite of [[see:right]].
Related to Latin [[same-root:rectus]], straight, making it a neat opposite of [[see:wrong]], crooked.
Related to [[same-root:wrong]].
Related to [[same-root:wrong]].
Related to [[same-root:wrong]].
Related to [[same-root:wrong]].
Related to [[same-root:wrong]]; intense fury and the sin of rage, and the usual Old English word for what we now call [[see:anger]].
Thought to be from Old Norse, a compound of not and ever, literally not ever; Swedish still says nej; compare Old English [[see:no]].
German word compared with [[see:nay]], showing n- added to make a negative.
Formed by putting n- before ever, like [[see:nay]].
Also a compound: Old English nā, from ne, not, plus a word meaning ever, the counterpart of Old Norse [[see:nay]].
Not one, another negative formed like [[see:no]] and [[see:never]].
Old Norse in origin but shouldn't have an L; [[see:Shakespeare]] back-formed it from [[from:groveling]], whose ending was misread as -ing.
Middle English adverb from Old Norse [[from:grúfa]], to be prone, plus the suffix [[from:-ling]]; it meant prone-like, later read as a participle.
Old English suffix making directional adverbs, seen in [[gave:groveling]], [[gave:sidelong]] and [[gave:headlong]]; unrelated to [[unrelated:long]].
Middle English sideling, from [[from:-ling]]; it means sidely or directed sideways rather than along the side.
Middle English headling, from [[from:-ling]], originally meaning headfirst.
Unrelated to the [[unrelated:-ling]] ending in headlong and sidelong, as is along.
A real, now lost adverb of the [[see:headlong]] type, which Rob would like to bring back.
Often credited with coining [[see:grovel]] in Henry VI, though he actually back-formed it from groveling.
Comparative ending added to already comparative adjectives, as in innermore, outermore and [[see:furthermore]]; thought to be from Scandinavian.
An example of the doubled comparative ending [[see:-more]].
Rob's home city in the Danelaw; with the Old Norse suffix [[from:-by]], it means place of the [[from:deer]], or of beasts.
Old Norse settlement suffix found in Danelaw places such as [[gave:Derby]] and [[gave:Grimsby]].
Another Danelaw town with the Old Norse suffix [[from:-by]].
Discussed before as once meaning any beast or animal, as in [[gave:Derby]], [[same-root:wilderness]] and [[see:Jura]].
The wild-deer-ness, the place where the beasts are, from [[from:deer]].
Scottish island known for whisky, whose name essentially means island of the beast, with the same first element as [[see:Derby]].
Old Norse place-name ending found in the old Danelaw, as in [[gave:Scunthorpe]].
A Danelaw town with the Old Norse ending [[from:-thorpe]].
Another Old Norse place-name ending in England, also found in American places named after British ones.
Old Norse place-name element meaning church, as in [[gave:Kirkwall]].
Old Norse for island, ending many island names around Britain such as [[gave:Orkney]], [[gave:Jersey]], [[gave:Guernsey]] and [[gave:Anglesey]].
Island group where [[see:Norn]] was spoken, which Rob is visiting; the name is thought to come from Old Norse for sea islands, with [[from:-ey]].
Scandinavian language of [[see:Orkney]] and Shetland, a variety of Norwegian that died out in the mid-1800s; the name means northern.
A hard name to use, since the Irish don't like being included under it.
Orkney's main town and airport; from [[from:kirk]], church, it means church inlet.
Channel island thought to be named after an unknown Viking, with [[from:-ey]], island.
Channel island thought to be named after an unknown Viking, with [[from:-ey]], island.
Island off Wales whose ending [[from:-ey]] means island; the meaning of the first part is unknown.
Hebridean island, known for whisky, whose name means misty island; Isle of Skye sounds lovely.
The Anglo-Saxon word for the sky generally, replaced by Old Norse [[see:sky]]; not as closely linked to [[see:haven]] as it looks.
From Old Norse, probably related to [[same-root?:harbor]], a sheltered place for a boat; the same word ends [[see:Copenhagen]].
Believed to be linked to [[same-root?:haven]]; both mean a place of shelter.
The -hagen at the end of the name is the same word as [[same-root:haven]].
Family dynasties in western Scotland, some set up by Norse settlers, such as [[see:MacIver]] and [[see:MacAulay]].
Scottish clan name meaning son of Ivar, a Norse name, combined with Gaelic [[from:Mac]].
Scottish name meaning son of Olaf, a hybrid of Gaelic [[from:Mac]] and a Scandinavian name.
Gaelic prefix meaning son of, making names like [[gave:MacIver]] and [[gave:MacAulay]] Gaelic-Norse hybrids.
